Simon Armitage’s ‘Remains’

Simon Armitage based ‘Remains’ on the real testimony of a soldier called Guardsman Tromans, who served in Iraq. The poem appeared in the 2008 documentary film The Not Dead, which explored PTSD in returning soldiers. The speaker describes shooting a looter in Basra and then being haunted by the memory of the killing, unable to wash the blood from his mind.

Key Fact

The poem is a dramatic monologue based on real testimony. Armitage uses colloquial, conversational language (“probably armed, possibly not”) to reflect how soldiers actually speak, making the psychological trauma feel authentic and immediate rather than literary or distant.

“probably armed, possibly not” — This devastating admission comes early. The soldier doesn’t know whether the man he killed was a threat. The modal verbs “probably” and “possibly” create uncertainty — and it is this uncertainty that torments him. The casual, almost throwaway delivery makes it more disturbing: this moral ambiguity is presented as routine.

“One of my mates goes by / and tosses his guts back into his body” — The brutal, graphic imagery strips away any dignity from death. The casual verb “tosses” is shocking — a human body is treated like rubbish. This reflects the dehumanising effect of war on both the dead and the living.

“his blood-shadow wanders the streets of his home town” — The compound noun “blood-shadow” and the image of the dead man “wandering” suggests the victim haunts the speaker. The dead man has followed the soldier home — he cannot escape what he has done, even in England.

“his bloody life in my bloody hands” — The repetition of “bloody” works as both literal description (blood on his hands) and colloquial swearing (expressing frustration). This double meaning captures the soldier’s guilt and anger simultaneously. He is responsible for a death he can never undo.

“I blink / and he bursts again through the doors of the bank” — The present tense “bursts” shows the memory replaying in real time. Every time the speaker blinks, the killing happens again. This is a powerful depiction of PTSD — the traumatic memory is involuntary, intrusive, and inescapable.

Structure of ‘Remains’

The poem begins with regular four-line stanzas, reflecting the soldier’s attempt to tell the story in an ordered, controlled way. But the final stanza breaks into just two lines: “his bloody life in my bloody hands.” The form literally breaks down as the soldier’s mental control collapses. The shift from past tense (the event) to present tense (the flashbacks) marks the poem’s turning point — the killing is over, but the trauma is ongoing.

Carol Ann Duffy’s ‘War Photographer’

Carol Ann Duffy wrote ‘War Photographer’ based on the experiences of real conflict photographers, particularly Don McCullin. The poem explores the moral tension between documenting suffering and the public’s indifference to it. The photographer develops his images in a darkroom in rural England, surrounded by peace, while the photographs reveal the horrors of war.

Key Fact

Duffy structures the poem around the contrast between “Rural England” (peaceful, indifferent) and the war zones the photographer has visited: “Belfast. Beirut. Phnom Penh.” The three-word list uses short, blunt proper nouns to represent real suffering, while England is associated with comfortable ignorance.

“In his darkroom he is finally alone / with spools of suffering set out in ordered rows” — The sibilance in “spools of suffering” creates a quiet, mournful tone. The metaphor of “ordered rows” echoes both film negatives and rows of graves — the photographs are records of death. “Finally alone” suggests he needs solitude to process what he has witnessed.

“a priest preparing to intone a Mass” — The simile compares the photographer’s work to a religious ritual. Developing photographs becomes a sacred act — a ceremony of remembrance for the dead. This elevates photography from journalism to something reverential and solemn.

“a half-formed ghost” — As the photograph develops in the chemical solution, the dead man’s face appears like a ghost. The image is both literal (the photograph developing) and metaphorical (the dead man haunting the photographer). This links to ‘Remains’ — both speakers are haunted by the dead.

“The reader’s eyeballs prick / with tears between the bath and pre-lunch beers” — The final stanza is bitterly ironic. The newspaper readers feel a momentary pang of emotion, but it is sandwiched between trivial domestic comforts. “Prick” suggests the emotion is tiny and superficial. Duffy criticises the public for their shallow response to real suffering.

Comparing Armitage and Duffy

Both poems explore the psychological aftermath of conflict, but from different perspectives. Armitage’s soldier is directly involved in the violence and cannot escape his guilt; Duffy’s photographer is a witness who feels the moral burden of documenting suffering that the public ignores. Both speakers are trapped: the soldier by flashbacks, the photographer by a cycle of documenting horror that changes nothing.

Structurally, Armitage uses colloquial language and broken form to mirror psychological breakdown; Duffy uses controlled stanzas and religious imagery to convey quiet, dignified grief. Both poems end without resolution — the trauma continues.

Imtiaz Dharker’s ‘Tissue’

Imtiaz Dharker uses paper as an extended metaphor for the fragility of human-made structures — buildings, borders, money, maps, and even identity. The poem argues that everything humans build is ultimately as thin and temporary as tissue paper. Dharker suggests this fragility should be embraced, not feared: if we built the world from paper, it would be “turned into your skin” — human and vulnerable rather than rigid and oppressive.

Key Fact

Dharker references the “Koran” (Qur’an) as “the kind of paper / thinned by age or touching.” This links the sacred text to the poem’s central argument: even holy scripture is physical, fragile paper that wears thin over time. Nothing humans create — not even religion — is permanent.

“Paper that lets the light / shine through” — The recurring image of light passing through paper suggests transparency and openness. Dharker argues that if structures (governments, borders) were transparent like paper, they would be more human and less oppressive. Light also symbolises truth and understanding — paper that “lets the light shine through” reveals rather than conceals.

“Maps too. The borderlines, the marks / that rivers make, roads, / railtracks, mountainfolds” — The listing technique collapses natural features (rivers, mountains) together with human constructs (roads, railtracks, borderlines). Dharker suggests that borders are as artificial as the paper they are drawn on — nature does not recognise human boundaries.

“turned into your skin” — The final twist reveals that the ultimate “tissue” is human skin. This shifts the poem from abstract philosophy to something deeply personal. Skin is the most fragile structure of all — and the most important. Dharker suggests that human vulnerability is more valuable than any building, border, or institution.

“might fly our lives like paper kites” — The simile imagines lives as paper kites: light, free, and joyful, but also fragile and at the mercy of the wind. This celebrates impermanence rather than fearing it. The image is playful and optimistic, contrasting with the poem’s earlier references to borders and money.

Structure of ‘Tissue’

The poem uses short, four-line stanzas that are themselves “thin” like tissue paper. The enjambment between stanzas creates a flowing, continuous movement — ideas spill across boundaries, just as the poem argues that human constructs should be more fluid. The final stanza is a single, isolated line (“turned into your skin”), standing alone on the page like a revelation. The form enacts the poem’s content: it is delicate, layered, and ultimately personal.

Jane Weir’s ‘Poppies’

Jane Weir wrote ‘Poppies’ from the perspective of a mother whose son has gone to war. The poem is set on Armistice Day and moves between the domestic (pinning a poppy to his blazer) and the battlefield (hoping to hear his voice “on the wind”). Weir was commissioned to write the poem for a 2009 anthology exploring the effects of conflict, and she chose to focus on the private grief of a parent rather than the public spectacle of war.

Key Fact

The poem does not specify which war or whether the son is alive or dead. This ambiguity is deliberate — the poem represents the universal experience of a parent losing a child to conflict. The domestic details (smoothing a blazer, making the cat hairs disappear) ground the poem in the everyday, making the grief more tangible.

“the poppy had crimped petals, the paper red / bleeding through their tissue paper white” — The poppy becomes a symbol linking remembrance (red poppy), blood (“bleeding”), and fragility (“tissue paper”). The verb “bleeding” is visceral — even the symbol of remembrance carries violence within it.

“Sellotape bandaged around my hand” — The domestic object (Sellotape) is compared to a bandage, linking household activities with the wounds of war. This textile imagery runs throughout the poem, connecting the mother’s domestic world with her son’s experience of conflict.

“I traced / the gilt wire trembling, crimped petals” — The mother touches the poppy delicately, as if touching her son. “Trembling” reveals her suppressed emotion. The sensory detail of touch makes the scene intensely personal and intimate.

“I listened, hoping to hear / your playground voice catching on the wind” — The final image is devastating. The mother goes to the war memorial and listens for her son’s childhood voice. “Playground voice” juxtaposes innocence with the reality of war. The separation between past (childhood) and present (conflict/death) is unbridgeable.

Comparing Dharker and Weir

Both poems use the fragility of paper/tissue as a central motif. Dharker uses it abstractly — paper represents all human constructs. Weir uses it concretely — the “tissue paper” of the poppy represents both remembrance and the fragility of human life. Both poems ultimately argue that human vulnerability is at the heart of everything: Dharker’s poem ends with “skin,” Weir’s with a mother’s love.

Structurally, Dharker uses short, thin stanzas that mirror paper; Weir uses longer, flowing stanzas that mirror the continuous stream of a mother’s memory. Both poets use enjambment to create flowing, uncontainable emotion.

Exam Technique — Anthology Comparison

This lesson covers the practical exam skills you need for the anthology comparison question: the typical format, timing, planning method and a bank of key quotations for all 15 poems in the Time and Place collection. Since this is a closed-book exam for your chosen poem (the named poem is printed), learning quotations is essential.

The Question Format

The anthology comparison question typically prints one named poem from the Time and Place collection and asks you to compare it with another poem of your choice from the same collection. A question might ask you to compare the ways the poets present feelings about a specific place, and to address the poets’ use of language, form and structure along with the influence of context on the poems. Your answer is assessed on AO2 (language, form, structure) and AO3 (context). Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the precise rubric wording and mark allocation.

Key Fact

The named poem is reprinted in the question paper, so you can quote directly from it. Your chosen poem is from memory — you must learn quotations. Aim for 2–3 short, versatile quotations per poem. Short quotations (3–6 words) are easier to memorise and more effective than long ones — they show you can select precisely.

Timing & Planning

Treat this question as a proportion of the whole paper — allocate time based on its share of the total marks. Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact timing; the breakdown below works for any block of roughly 35–40 minutes, but you can scale it to the time you are given.

First sixth of your time: Read the named poem carefully. Choose your second poem. Write a one-sentence thesis. Jot down 3 comparison points with quotations for each poem.

Middle section (writing): Write 3–4 paragraphs of integrated comparison. Each paragraph = one comparison point, weaving both poems together, with AO2 analysis dominant and AO3 woven in.

Final few minutes: Re-read your answer. Check you have addressed both AO2 and AO3. Add any missed comparative connectives. Fix spelling errors in quotations.

1. Thesis: Write one sentence stating how both poems approach the question’s focus — include a similarity AND a difference.

2. Point 1 (Language): Name one language feature per poem (e.g. Blake’s anaphora “every” / Afrika’s bodily language “my feet know”). Note the effect of each.

3. Point 2 (Form/Structure): Name the form of each poem and explain what it does (e.g. Blake’s quatrains = controlled rage / Afrika’s clipped free verse = suppressed anger).

4. Point 3 (Context): One context point per poem that explains WHY the poet presents place this way.

5. Chosen poem quotations: Write out 2–3 key quotations from memory so you don’t forget them mid-essay.

Key Quotation Bank — All 15 Poems

Learn 2–3 short quotations per poem. Focus on quotations that contain analysable language features — metaphors, imagery, structural devices — not plain narrative statements.

To Autumn (Keats): “Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness” (sibilance, sensory richness) • “Where are the songs of Spring?” (rhetorical question, acceptance of time passing) • “soft-dying day” (gentle euphemism for decline/death)

Composed upon Westminster Bridge (Wordsworth): “Earth has not anything to show more fair” (hyperbole, awe) • “like a garment, wear / The beauty of the morning” (simile, city clothed in nature) • “the very houses seem asleep” (personification, peace)

London (Blake): “charter’d street” / “charter’d Thames” (repetition, control) • “mind-forg’d manacles” (metaphor, psychological oppression) • “Marriage hearse” (oxymoron, corruption)

I started Early – Took my Dog (Dickinson): “He followed – close behind” (personification, pursuit) • “I felt His Silver Heel / Upon my Ankle” (sensory, threatening intimacy) • Hymn metre creating unsettling contrast

Where the Picnic was (Hardy): “the charred stick-ends of our last year’s fire” (symbol, dead memory) • “winter mire” (pathetic fallacy) • “they are scattered” (loss of community)

Adlestrop (Thomas): “Yes, I remember Adlestrop” (conversational, intimate) • “all the birds / Of Oxfordshire and Gloucestershire” (expansion, pastoral beauty) • “no one left and no one came” (isolation, stillness)

Home Thoughts from Abroad (Browning): “Oh, to be in England / Now that April’s there!” (exclamatory longing) • “the wise thrush; he sings each song twice over” (personification, joy) • “gaudy melon-flower” (foreign beauty dismissed)

First Flight (Fanthorpe): Landscape shrinking during takeoff (perspective shift as metaphor) • Familiar details becoming abstract (loss through distance)

Stewart Island (Adcock): “a raft of resting shags” (precise observation) • Speaker as visitor, not native • Free verse reflecting casual, detached exploration

Presents from my Aunts in Pakistan (Alvi): “of no fixed nationality” (dual identity) • “peacock-blue” / “apple-green” (colour imagery for Pakistani culture) • “longed / for denim and corduroy” (English items colourless)

Hurricane Hits England (Nichols): “the earth is the earth is the earth” (epizeuxis, universal connection) • “Huracan,” “Oya,” “Shango” (invocation of Caribbean gods) • Pronoun shift from “her” to “I”

Nothing’s Changed (Afrika): “my feet know / and my hands” (bodily memory) • “the hot, white, inward turning / anger of my eyes” (controlled rage) • Restaurant vs café contrast (inequality made visible)

Postcard from a Travel Snob (Hannah): Persona voice (dramatic irony) • Rhyming couplets (polished surface mirroring pretension) • Satirical tone exposing how place is used for ego

In Romney Marsh (Davidson): “organ stops / Pealing a low-tide psalm” (extended organ metaphor) • ABAB quatrains (hymn-like, worshipful) • Nature as grand and indifferent

Absence (Jennings): “I am the one whose want / Has made this landscape poorer” (grief changes the landscape) • Double meaning of “want” (desire + lack) • Tight tercets (compressed emotion)

Key Fact

You do not need to memorise long passages. Short, precise quotations (3–6 words) are more effective because you can embed them into your sentences: “Blake’s ‘mind-forg’d manacles’ suggests…” is smoother and more analytical than copying out a full stanza. Accuracy matters — a slightly misquoted word can undermine your credibility.

Choosing Your Comparison Poem

Before the exam, prepare 3–4 “go-to” poems that you know in depth. For each, know: the form, 2–3 key quotations, 2 language features, 1 context point. The table below suggests strong pairings by theme:

Celebrating place: To Autumn + Westminster Bridge + Adlestrop + Home Thoughts from Abroad

Social criticism: London + Nothing’s Changed

Displacement: Presents from my Aunts + Hurricane Hits England + Stewart Island

Memory and loss: Where the Picnic was + First Flight + Absence + Adlestrop

Nature’s power: I started Early + In Romney Marsh + To Autumn + Hurricane Hits England

The Impact of War on Others

While some conflict poems focus on soldiers in battle, others explore the ripple effects of war on those who were never on the front line: the mothers who wait, the children who grow up in the shadow of conflict, and the communities destroyed by violence. These poems remind us that war’s damage extends far beyond the battlefield.

The poets in this group use different perspectives — a mother at home, a photographer processing images, a speaker addressing a distant conflict — to show that war is not just a military event but a human catastrophe that touches everyone. The shift in perspective from soldier to civilian is itself a political act: it challenges the idea that war is only the business of those who fight.

Key Fact

The “impact of war on others” poems focus on three groups: families left behind (grief, absence, waiting), witnesses who see war’s consequences (photographers, journalists, bystanders), and communities affected by displacement, destruction, and lasting trauma. These poems shift the focus from heroism to suffering.

War Photographer — Carol Ann Duffy (1985)

Duffy’s poem follows a war photographer developing his photographs in a darkroom after returning from a conflict zone. The poem contrasts the “ordered rows” of film spools with the chaos they contain, and the “Rural England” of the photographer’s home with the war zones he has witnessed. The opening simile — spools “ordered rows” are “as though this were a church and he / a priest preparing to intone a Mass” — gives the darkroom a sacred quality, as if developing photographs is a religious act of witnessing.

The poem’s most powerful moment comes when an image develops: “A half-formed ghost begins to twist before his eyes, / a stranger’s features / faintly start to materialise.” The ghost metaphor suggests the subject is already dead — captured only as a haunting trace. The final stanza delivers Duffy’s critique: the readers back in England see the photos but “do not care” — they feel a momentary pang before turning to the next page. The poem indicts comfortable indifference to suffering.

“The reader’s eyeballs prick / with tears between the bath and pre-lunch beers.” Duffy uses the mundane domestic routine (“bath,” “pre-lunch beers”) to expose the shallow sympathy of newspaper readers. The juxtaposition of comfortable routine with war photography creates a damning contrast: other people’s suffering becomes a brief interruption in a comfortable life. “Eyeballs prick with tears” suggests the response is physical but superficial — a momentary reaction, not a genuine engagement with suffering.

The Emigrée — Carol Rumens (1993)

Rumens’s poem is spoken by someone who left their homeland as a child, probably fleeing conflict or political oppression. The speaker remembers the city with idealised, sunlit nostalgia: “There once was a country… I left it as a child” — the fairy-tale opening suggests the memory has been preserved in a childlike, golden light. Despite hearing that the city is now “sick with tyrants,” the speaker’s memory remains stubbornly positive: “my city takes me dancing.”

The poem explores how conflict creates displacement that lasts a lifetime. The speaker’s language is caught between two worlds: they still carry the “original view” of their city even though that city may no longer exist. The final stanza’s image of the city “branded” on their hands suggests identity is physically marked by the place you come from — conflict cannot erase it, even when it destroys the place itself.

Key Fact

Rumens shows conflict’s lasting impact through three ideas: the speaker’s idealised memory refuses to accept the city’s destruction, their identity remains “branded” by a homeland they can never return to, and the gap between past beauty and present violence creates a permanent emotional displacement.

Comparing Impact Poems

Similarity: Both poems explore the gap between direct experience of conflict and the distance of safety. Both speakers carry war’s images with them — the photographer through film, the emigrée through memory.

Difference: Duffy critiques those who are indifferent to suffering; Rumens explores how a victim of conflict preserves their identity. Duffy’s tone is angry and accusatory; Rumens’s is nostalgic and defiant.

Context: Both poets write about late 20th-century conflicts where media coverage brought images of war into comfortable Western homes. Duffy responds to this media saturation; Rumens responds to the refugee experience of displacement and memory.

Love Across the Anthology

The WJEC Eduqas poetry anthology explores love in strikingly different ways. Five poems tackle this theme directly: Elizabeth Barrett Browning’s Sonnet 43, Lord Byron’s She Walks in Beauty, Carol Ann Duffy’s Valentine, Rita Dove’s Cozy Apologia, and Simon Armitage’s The Manhunt. Together they show that love is not one emotion but many — passionate, idealising, unconventional, comfortable, and damaged.

Sonnet 43 — Elizabeth Barrett Browning

Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote Sonnet 43 as part of the Sonnets from the Portuguese (1850), a sequence of 44 love poems addressed to her husband Robert Browning. She composed them secretly during their courtship, at a time when her domineering father forbade all his children from marrying. The poem is a declaration of total, all-encompassing devotion.

Key Fact

The poem’s opening question — “How do I love thee? Let me count the ways” — attempts to measure something immeasurable. Browning lists love that reaches “the depth and breadth and height / My soul can reach,” love “to the level of every day’s / Most quiet need,” and love given “freely” and “purely.” The anaphora of “I love thee” builds cumulative intensity.

Key quotations: The spatial imagery — “depth and breadth and height” — makes love three-dimensional, filling all available space. The reference to loving “with the passion put to use / In my old griefs” suggests that the energy once spent on suffering is now redirected into love. The final line — “I shall but love thee better after death” — pushes love beyond mortality, linking it to religious faith.

Browning uses the Petrarchan sonnet form, traditionally associated with male poets addressing an idealised, unattainable woman. By adopting this form as a woman speaking to her husband, Browning subverts the tradition — the female voice claims authority over the love poem. The iambic pentameter creates a calm, measured tone, reflecting the certainty of her devotion rather than the anguish typical of earlier sonnets.

She Walks in Beauty — Lord Byron

Lord Byron reportedly wrote She Walks in Beauty (1814) after seeing his cousin Anne Wilmot at a party, dressed in black mourning clothes with spangles. The poem idealises the woman’s appearance, blending light and darkness to create an image of perfect harmony.

Key quotations: The opening simile — “She walks in beauty, like the night / Of cloudless climes and starry skies” — is striking because beauty is usually compared to daylight, not darkness. Byron finds beauty in the balance: “all that’s best of dark and bright / Meet in her aspect and her eyes.” The repeated long vowel sounds (“cloudless climes,” “starry skies”) create a musical, awestruck tone. The woman’s external beauty reflects internal goodness: “A mind at peace with all below, / A heart whose love is innocent.”

Byron uses a regular ABABAB rhyme scheme and iambic tetrameter, giving the poem a musical, almost hymn-like quality. The antithesis of light and dark runs throughout — “dark and bright,” “day denies,” “raven tress” against “softly lightens.” The woman exists in a liminal space between opposites, and this balance is what makes her beautiful. The speaker remains at a distance throughout: he observes but never touches or possesses.

Valentine — Carol Ann Duffy

Carol Ann Duffy wrote Valentine (1993) as a deliberate rejection of commercial romance. Instead of roses or satin hearts, the speaker offers an onion as a love gift — an extended metaphor that captures love’s complexity: its intensity, its ability to cause tears, its layers, and its potential to wound.

Key Fact

The onion symbolises multiple aspects of love: it makes you cry (emotional pain), has layers (complexity), can blind you with tears (love as overwhelming), and its scent “clings to your fingers” and “clings to your knife” (love is possessive, even dangerous). Duffy deliberately replaces sentimental clichés with an image that is honest about love’s darker side.

Key quotations: “Not a red rose or a satin heart” — the opening negatives reject commercial Valentine’s Day. “It will blind you with tears / like a lover” — love causes pain. The final image — “Its scent will cling to your fingers, / cling to your knife” — introduces threat. The word “knife” ends the poem on a violent note, suggesting possessiveness or the aftermath of a relationship’s end.

Cozy Apologia — Rita Dove

Rita Dove wrote Cozy Apologia (2004) for her husband Fred during a hurricane. The title is an “apology” for writing about comfortable, mature love rather than dramatic passion. The poem contrasts settled domestic happiness with the speaker’s youthful romantic fantasies about “skinny-pinching” teenage boys who were “dark knights” on borrowed steeds.

Key quotations: “I could pick anything and think of you” — love permeates ordinary life. The hurricane outside provides a backdrop that makes domestic safety feel precious: “I’m still / as a cicada shell.” The simile suggests the speaker has outgrown her former self, leaving behind an empty shell of adolescent fantasy for something real.

The Manhunt — Simon Armitage

Simon Armitage wrote The Manhunt (2007) from the perspective of Laura, the wife of Eddie Beddoes, a soldier who returned from Bosnia with severe physical and psychological injuries. The poem traces the wife’s gradual, patient attempt to reconnect with her damaged husband — both physically and emotionally.

Key quotations: “After the first phase, / after passionate nights” — the relationship has stages; intimacy returns slowly. The body is described through military and industrial metaphors: “frozen river which ran through his face,” “the damaged, porcelain collar-bone.” These suggest fragility beneath a tough exterior. The final image — “only then did I come close” — uses the phrase “come close” ambiguously: physical proximity and emotional understanding.

Idealised vs realistic love: Browning and Byron present love as wholly positive and transcendent. Duffy and Armitage show its painful, difficult side. Dove occupies a middle ground — love as comforting but unglamorous.

The speaker’s position: In Sonnet 43 and Valentine, the speaker addresses their lover directly. In She Walks in Beauty, Byron observes from a distance. In The Manhunt, the wife narrates her attempt to reach a withdrawn partner. These different positions shape how we experience each love relationship.

Traditional vs subversive forms: Browning uses the Petrarchan sonnet but gives the woman the speaking voice. Byron uses regular metre and rhyme. Duffy and Armitage use free verse to reflect the unconventional nature of the love they describe.

Key Fact

Both Sonnet 43 and Valentine are declarations of love from a female speaker, but they differ radically in tone: Browning’s is earnest and spiritual, while Duffy’s is deliberately anti-romantic, using an onion to expose love’s painful layers alongside its sweetness.

Exam Day Preparation

This final lesson brings together everything you have learned across the collection. Your anthology comparison question will test your ability to select, compare and analyse two poems under timed conditions. The challenge is not just knowledge — it is making fast, confident decisions about which poem to choose and what to write about. This lesson gives you the tools to do that: a decision-making framework, a complete quotation bank for all 15 poems, and strategies for writing under pressure.

The Question Format

Anthology comparison questions typically follow a similar pattern: you are asked to compare how poets present a given theme or aspect of relationships in a named poem and one other poem from your studied collection. The named poem is usually printed in full on the question paper. You choose the second poem from memory. You are assessed on AO2 (language, form and structure) and AO3 (context). Check your exam board’s specimen paper for the exact wording, mark allocations and recommended timings.

Key Fact

You do not need to prepare all 15 poems equally. Choose 4–5 poems that you know deeply — these become your “go-to” choices for any question. A well-analysed poem you know thoroughly will always outscore a poem you half-remember. Quality of analysis beats breadth of knowledge.

Choosing Your Comparison Poem: A Decision Framework

When you see the named poem and the theme, ask yourself three questions:

1. Which of my prepared poems connects to this theme? If the theme is “loss,” your options include “Neutral Tones,” “A Complaint,” “One Flesh,” “La Belle Dame Sans Merci.” If it is “power,” consider “My Last Duchess,” “Valentine,” “The Manhunt.”

2. Can I identify both similarities AND differences? The best comparisons have both. A poem that is simply “the same” as the named poem gives you less to say than one with interesting contrasts in method, tone or context.

3. Can I discuss form and structure, not just language? If your only point is about imagery, you are missing AO2 marks. Choose a poem where you can compare form (sonnet vs free verse), structure (cyclical vs linear) or voice (dramatic monologue vs first person).

Idealised / passionate love: Sonnet 43 + She Walks in Beauty + La Belle Dame Sans Merci + i wanna be yours

Love gone wrong / loss: Neutral Tones + A Complaint + One Flesh + La Belle Dame Sans Merci

Power and control: My Last Duchess + Valentine + The Manhunt

Family / protection: A Child to his Sick Grandfather + Nettles + My Father Would Not Show Us

Modern / everyday love: 1st Date She/He + i wanna be yours + Love’s Dog + Valentine

Distance / emotional barriers: A Complaint + One Flesh + The Manhunt + My Father Would Not Show Us + Neutral Tones

Quotation Bank: All 15 Poems

Below are 3–4 key quotations per poem. For your chosen “go-to” poems, memorise all of these. For the others, know at least one. Each quotation is paired with its main analytical focus.

La Belle Dame Sans Merci (Keats):

• “Full beautiful — a faery’s child” — supernatural, idealised beauty (AO2: imagery). • “La Belle Dame sans Merci / Thee hath in thrall” — love as enslavement (AO2: metaphor). • “Alone and palely loitering” — devastation after love’s loss (AO2: pathetic fallacy). • “And no birds sing” — cyclical refrain, nature emptied (AO2: structure).

A Child to his Sick Grandfather (Baillie):

• “Your head, it shakes so sore” — innocent directness cataloguing decline (AO2: voice). • “You shall have my chair” — child’s inadequate comfort (AO2: dramatic irony). • Rhyming couplets — nursery-rhyme quality contrasts with death (AO2: form).

She Walks in Beauty (Byron):

• “She walks in beauty, like the night / Of cloudless climes and starry skies” — beauty compared to darkness (AO2: simile). • “One shade the more, one ray the less” — perfect balance (AO2: antithesis). • “A mind at peace with all below, / A heart whose love is innocent” — inner beauty (AO2: structure — external to internal).

A Complaint (Wordsworth):

• “A fountain at my fond heart’s door” — love as visible abundance (AO2: extended metaphor). • “A well of love — it may be deep” — dashes create doubt (AO2: punctuation). • Three-stanza structure: past, present, reflection (AO2: structure).

Neutral Tones (Hardy):

• “The sun was white, as though chidden of God” — drained, punished landscape (AO2: pathetic fallacy). • “Your eyes on me were as eyes that rove / Over tedious riddles” — boredom and indifference (AO2: simile). • “And a pond edged with greyish leaves” — cyclical return to the scene (AO2: structure).

My Last Duchess (Browning):

• “That’s my last Duchess painted on the wall” — possessive pronoun, ownership (AO2: word choice). • “I gave commands; / Then all smiles stopped together” — euphemism for murder (AO2: understatement). • “Looking as if she were alive” — casually menacing (AO2: dramatic irony). • Single-stanza dramatic monologue (AO2: form).

Sonnet 43 (Barrett Browning):

• “How do I love thee? Let me count the ways” — quantifying the unquantifiable (AO2: rhetorical question). • “I love thee to the depth and breadth and height / My soul can reach” — spatial metaphor for limitless love (AO2: imagery). • “I shall but love thee better after death” — love transcending mortality (AO2: volta). • Petrarchan sonnet form — female poet subverting male tradition (AO3: context).

1st Date She/He (Cope): • Dual perspective — both sides of dating anxiety (AO2: structure). • Colloquial inner monologue (AO2: voice).

Valentine (Duffy): • “Not a red rose or a satin heart” — rejecting clichés (AO2: opening). • “It will blind you with tears” — love causes pain (AO2: metaphor). • “Its scent will cling to your fingers, / cling to your knife” — darkening to violence (AO2: tone shift).

One Flesh (Jennings): • “Lying apart now, each in a separate bed” — physical and emotional distance (AO2: imagery). • “Tossed up like flotsam from a former passion” — wreckage of love (AO2: simile). • “Strangely apart, yet strangely close together” — paradox (AO2: language). • “Whose fire from which I came, has now grown cold?” — unsettling final question (AO2: volta).

i wanna be yours (Cooper Clarke): • “I wanna be your vacuum cleaner / breathing in your dust” — domestic devotion (AO2: metaphor). • “I will not run out” — sincere constancy (AO2: tone shift). • Anaphora of “I wanna be your” — hypnotic repetition (AO2: structure).

Love’s Dog (Hatfield): • “What I love about love is its / What I hate about love is its” — love as paradox (AO2: structure). • Oxymorons throughout (AO2: language).

Nettles (Scannell): • “A regiment of spite” — military semantic field (AO2: imagery). • “Tall as soldiers” — nettles regrow, protection is futile (AO2: metaphor). • Single stanza, blank verse (AO2: form).

The Manhunt (Armitage): • “The damaged, porcelain collar-bone” — fragile beauty (AO2: juxtaposition). • “The frozen river which ran through his face” — scar as landscape (AO2: metaphor). • “Only then would he let me” — gradual access (AO2: structure). • Inward journey: external wounds to hidden PTSD (AO2: structure).

My Father Would Not Show Us (de Kok): • “Would not show us,” “would not let us see” — repeated negatives (AO2: language). • Free verse with irregular lines (AO2: form). • The body as concealed text (AO2: imagery).

Key Fact

The strongest students walk into the exam with 3–4 pre-planned comparison pairings. For example: “If they ask about loss, I’ll compare with Neutral Tones. If they ask about power, I’ll compare with My Last Duchess. If they ask about family, I’ll compare with Nettles.” Adapt these to the specific question wording, but having a starting point saves valuable planning time.

Writing Under Pressure: Final Checklist

Before writing: Read the question twice. Identify the theme. Choose your poem. Plan 3 points (each covering both poems). While writing: Start every paragraph with a comparative point. Quote from both poems (the named poem from the paper, your chosen poem from memory). Analyse how (AO2), not just what. Weave in context (AO3). After writing: Check you have discussed both poems in every paragraph. Check you have mentioned form or structure at least once. Check for spelling and punctuation.

War Beyond the Battlefield

Not all conflict poetry is written from the soldier’s perspective. Three poems in the Edexcel Conflict anthology focus on the people left behind or affected indirectly: Poppies by Jane Weir explores a mother’s grief as her son leaves for war; War Photographer by Carole Satyamurti examines how witnessing conflict through a lens creates moral and emotional conflict; and What Were They Like? by Denise Levertov asks what happens to an entire culture when it is destroyed by war.

Key Fact

Jane Weir’s Poppies was commissioned by the Poetry Archive in 2009 as part of a collection responding to conflict. It draws on the experience of mothers whose children serve in the armed forces, and blends domestic imagery with the symbolism of Remembrance Day.

Poppies — Jane Weir

The poem is narrated by a mother who pins a poppy on her son’s lapel before he leaves — possibly for war, possibly for the last time. The domestic details are heartbreaking: she resists the urge to “run my fingers through the gelled / blackthorns of your hair” and later smooths down his “shirt’s upturned collar.” These small, physical gestures convey a love she cannot express in words.

Weir uses a extended metaphor of textiles throughout: “I pinned one onto your lapel, crimped petals,” “sellotape bandaged around my hand,” “the world overflowing like a treasure chest.” The textile imagery connects the mother’s domestic world (sewing, fabric) to the military world (the poppy, the bandage). The word “crimped” suggests something carefully made by hand — fragile, easily damaged.

The poem ends with the mother at a war memorial, pressing her ear against it “hoping to hear / your playground voice catching on the wind.” The enjambment here mirrors her reaching out emotionally across the distance. “Playground voice” reminds us he is still her child, regardless of his age, and the verb “catching” suggests the voice is fragile and fleeting, barely there.

Weir deliberately blurs the timeline. The poem shifts between memories of the son as a child (“playground voice,” “All Hallows’ Day”) and the present moment of him leaving. This non-linear structure reflects how grief works — the mother’s mind moves between past and present, unable to separate the child she raised from the soldier he has become. The lack of a clear narrative resolution mirrors the unresolved nature of her grief.

War Photographer — Carole Satyamurti

Satyamurti’s War Photographer (not to be confused with Carol Ann Duffy’s poem of the same title) presents a photographer who documents conflict zones. The poem explores the moral dilemma of witnessing suffering: should the photographer help, or does their role demand they remain detached and document the truth?

The photographer captures an image of a dying man: “The reassurance of the viewfinder, / the smells of chemicals and ordinary life.” The “viewfinder” acts as a barrier between the photographer and reality — a protective frame that allows them to cope. Yet the “reassurance” is fragile: the photographs force them to confront what they witnessed later, in the safety of the darkroom.

Satyamurti uses the metaphor of the camera as a “reflecting eye” — it mirrors reality but also distances the viewer from it. The poem questions whether photography can truly convey suffering, or whether it reduces human agony to a flat, consumable image. This links to AO3: the role of media in shaping public understanding of conflict.

What Were They Like? — Denise Levertov (1966)

Levertov wrote this poem in protest against the Vietnam War. It is structured as a Q&A: six numbered questions about Vietnamese culture are followed by six numbered answers. The questions ask about Vietnamese customs, art, ceremonies and language. The answers reveal that all of it has been destroyed.

The Q&A format is clinically detached — it reads like an anthropological survey about an extinct civilisation. This is deliberate: Levertov forces the reader to confront the idea that an entire living culture has been reduced to a historical curiosity. The past tense throughout (“Did they use bone and ivory?”) treats the Vietnamese as already gone, which is both accusatory and deeply unsettling.

Key Fact

Levertov’s answers grow increasingly emotional: “Sir, laughter is bitter to the burned mouth.” The word “Sir” is formally polite but also accusatory — it addresses the powerful people who ordered the destruction. The metaphor “bitter to the burned mouth” is visceral, connecting the physical horror of napalm to the death of joy itself.

Grief (Poppies): Weir focuses on individual, private loss — one mother’s unspoken love for her child. The conflict is internal: the struggle between letting go and holding on.

Moral conflict (War Photographer): Satyamurti explores the ethical tension between documenting suffering and being complicit in it. The photographer’s conflict is professional and personal.

Cultural erasure (What Were They Like?): Levertov addresses the largest scale — the destruction of an entire people’s identity. The conflict is political and collective.

All three poems show that war’s damage extends far beyond the battlefield. In the exam, comparing the scale of impact (individual vs collective) is a strong analytical move.

Loss & Distance — Four Poems

These poems explore what happens when love is lost, ended, or separated by distance or death. Each poet handles absence differently: Byron with grief, Hardy with bitterness, Doshi with quiet connection, and Causley with serene acceptance.

“When We Two Parted” — Byron (Revisited)

Byron’s speaker is trapped in unresolved grief. The cyclical structure (“silence and tears” opening and closing) creates a sense that the pain has not diminished. The poem’s power lies in its restraint: the speaker cannot publicly grieve because the affair was secret. This forced silence intensifies the emotional damage. The half-rhymes (“morning”/“warning”) create a sense of incompleteness, reflecting the unfinished grief.

“Neutral Tones” — Thomas Hardy (1867)

Hardy describes the moment he realised a love affair was over. The setting is bleak: “We stood by a pond that winter day, / And the sun was white, as though chidden of God.” The pathetic fallacy is powerful — the “white” sun suggests something drained of warmth and life, and the phrase “chidden of God” (scolded by God) implies even God has turned away.

The woman’s smile is described as “the deadest thing / Alive enough to have strength to die.” This oxymoron — something both dead and alive — captures the painful zombie-state of a dying relationship. The poem ends with the image returning: “And a pond edged with greyish leaves.” Like Byron, Hardy uses cyclical structure to trap the speaker in the memory of loss.

Key Fact

Hardy’s “the deadest thing / Alive enough to have strength to die” captures the painful state of a relationship that is dying but not yet dead. The oxymoron makes the reader feel the exhaustion and bitterness of love turning to indifference.

“Letters from Yorkshire” — Maura Doshi (2002)

Doshi presents a long-distance relationship sustained by letters. The speaker (in a city) receives news from a man in Yorkshire who describes digging his garden and seeing “the first lapwings.” His physical, outdoor life contrasts with her indoor, desk-bound existence. Yet the letters create a genuine connection: “Is it enough to say that what he sees / I see?”

The poem questions whether emotional connection can survive physical distance. Doshi’s answer is yes: “our souls tap out messages across the icy miles.” The word “souls” elevates the connection beyond the physical, and the synaesthesia-like image of souls “tapping” messages blends the physical (tapping) with the spiritual (souls), suggesting communication that transcends technology.

Causley imagines his dead parents waiting for him on the other side of a stream — a boundary between life and death. The scene is idyllic: his mother spreads a picnic cloth, his father has “the same suit / Of Survey tweed.” The precise, mundane details (the “H.P. sauce bottle,” the “tin of pears”) make the scene feel real and comforting rather than frightening.

The final lines — “I had not thought it would be like this” — suggest that death is not the terrifying void we fear but a reunion with loved ones. The stream separating the speaker from his parents is a traditional symbol of the boundary between life and death. Causley’s tone is serene, not grief-stricken — he presents death as something gentle and familiar.

Key Fact

Causley uses precise, everyday details (H.P. sauce, tweed suit, tin of pears) to make the afterlife vision feel familiar and safe. Death is not frightening but a return to the warmth and normality of childhood — a reunion rather than an ending.

Byron vs Hardy: Both present the end of love through bleak imagery and cyclical structure. Byron is grief-stricken and secret; Hardy is bitter and disillusioned. Byron’s love was passionate; Hardy’s has drained to nothing.

Doshi vs Causley: Both present love surviving distance or separation. Doshi’s lovers are separated by geography; Causley’s by death. Both suggest that love transcends physical boundaries — but Doshi’s tone is questioning while Causley’s is serene.

Hardy vs Causley: Hardy presents love’s end as bleak and bitter (drained colour, dead smile); Causley presents death as warm and comforting (picnic, familiar details). Opposite emotional responses to loss.

705185df-1eb7-4748-90d9-b1b32c60187c.content_html:
“Porphyria’s Lover” — Robert Browning (1836)

Browning’s dramatic monologue presents a deeply disturbing speaker who murders his lover Porphyria to preserve the perfect moment of her devotion. The poem opens with pathetic fallacy: “The rain set early in tonight, / The sullen wind was soon awake.” The storm mirrors the speaker’s inner turmoil. When Porphyria arrives, she brings warmth and light: she “made the cheerless grate / Blaze up.”

The speaker realises that Porphyria truly loves him: “That moment she was mine, mine, fair, / Perfectly pure and good.” The repetition of “mine” reveals his possessiveness. He then strangles her with her own hair: “I found / A thing to do, and all her hair / In one long yellow string I wound / Three times her little throat around, / And strangled her.” The casual, matter-of-fact tone is chilling. He shows no remorse: “And yet God has not said a word!” — he believes God approves, or at least does not object.

Key Fact

Browning uses the dramatic monologue to expose the speaker’s distorted logic: he murders Porphyria to “preserve” her love. The repetition of “mine” reveals possessiveness, the calm tone reveals psychopathy, and the final line suggests he believes himself justified. Desire here is controlling, violent, and fatal.

“The Farmer’s Bride” — Charlotte Mew (1916)

Mew’s dramatic monologue presents a farmer whose young wife is terrified of him and of physical intimacy. The farmer married her young: “Three Summers since I chose a maid.” The word “chose” suggests she had no say — marriage as transaction, not partnership. When she ran away, the villagers caught her “like a hare” — the simile reduces the wife to a hunted animal.

The wife is described through nature imagery: “like a mouse,” “like a leveret,” “Her eyes, her hair, her hair!” The farmer’s desire is unrequited — she fears him, and he cannot bridge the gap. The final stanza shifts to desperate, almost threatening desire: “Oh! my God! the down, / The soft young down of her, the brown, / The brown of her — her eyes, her hair, her hair!” The fragmented, breathless repetition suggests his self-control is breaking. Mew leaves the ending ambiguous and ominous.

Nagra presents a joyful, playful depiction of desire in a British-Indian marriage. The speaker is a young Sikh shopkeeper who neglects his father’s shop to be with his new wife upstairs. The poem is full of humour and energy: “my bride / she effing at my mum / in all di colours of Punjabi.” The phonetic English (“di” for “the”) creates a distinctive dialect voice that blends Punjabi and English.

The desire here is healthy, mutual, and joyful — a complete contrast to Browning and Mew. The couple sit on the shop steps “watching my bride — making chapatti after chapatti.” The mundane domestic detail (chapattis) is presented with the same delight as the moonlit description of her face: “her eyes are black kohl / her hair is Toronto plane-Loss.” Nagra celebrates multicultural British identity and presents desire as fun, equal, and life-affirming.

Key Fact

Three poems, three types of desire: Browning’s is possessive and fatal, Mew’s is frustrated and potentially dangerous, and Nagra’s is mutual, playful, and life-affirming. The exam often asks about “how desire is presented” — these three provide powerful contrasts.

Browning vs Mew: Both use dramatic monologues to reveal speakers whose desire is controlling. Both objectify women. But Browning’s speaker acts (murder); Mew’s is still restraining himself (the ending is ambiguous). Both expose how patriarchal power distorts desire.

Browning vs Nagra: Maximum contrast — Browning’s desire is possessive, violent, and one-sided; Nagra’s is mutual, joyful, and equal. Browning’s woman is silenced (literally killed); Nagra’s wife is loud, funny, and independent.

Mew vs Nagra: Both present marriage, but Mew’s is a prison (the wife is trapped) and Nagra’s is a celebration (the couple choose each other). Mew’s wife is silent and animal-like; Nagra’s wife is vocal and vibrant.

Nature & the Self

The final two individual poems we study take very different approaches to the relationship between place and the self. Dickinson’s “I started Early – Took my Dog” presents nature as a powerful, almost threatening force, while Hannah’s “Postcard from a Travel Snob” uses the voice of a pretentious traveller to satirise attitudes to place. Together, these poems explore how we project our own feelings, fears and prejudices onto the places we visit.

I started Early – Took my Dog — Emily Dickinson

Dickinson (1830–1886) was an American poet who lived a reclusive life in Amherst, Massachusetts. She published fewer than a dozen poems in her lifetime; nearly 1,800 were discovered after her death. “I started Early – Took my Dog” describes a walk to the sea. At first, the speaker observes calmly: “the Mermaids in the Basement / Came out to look at me.” But the sea gradually becomes aggressive, rising around the speaker like a pursuer: “He followed – close behind – / I felt His Silver Heel / Upon my Ankle.”

Dickinson personifies the sea as male (“He”) and the encounter feels increasingly like a pursuit or even an assault. The sea “ate the Miles” and reached “my Apron – and my Belt.” The speaker only escapes when “the Tide went past the Town” and she reaches safety. The poem can be read as an allegory for many things — the power of nature over humanity, the threat of male dominance, or the overwhelming force of desire or creativity.

Key Fact

Dickinson personifies the sea as “He” — a male pursuer whose power the speaker cannot control. This gendered personification allows multiple interpretations: the sea as nature’s overwhelming force, as threatening masculinity or as uncontrollable creative inspiration. The poem works on both a literal level (a walk to the beach) and a symbolic level (an encounter with something bigger than the self).

Dickinson’s poems are famous for their dashes, which interrupt the rhythm and create pauses that feel like gasps or hesitations: “I started Early – Took my Dog –.” The poem uses hymn metre (common metre) — alternating lines of eight and six syllables — which gives it a deceptively simple, song-like quality. This simplicity contrasts with the poem’s disturbing content, creating an unsettling effect: a nursery-rhyme rhythm tells a story about being chased by the sea.

Postcard from a Travel Snob — Sophie Hannah

Hannah (born 1971) is a contemporary British poet and novelist. “Postcard from a Travel Snob” is written in the voice of a persona — a pretentious traveller who mocks tourists for visiting “obvious” destinations. The speaker boasts about their own obscure, off-the-beaten-track location and sneers at those who holiday in popular places: the implication is that the speaker’s travel choices make them culturally superior.

The poem is satirical. Hannah does not agree with the speaker — she exposes the travel snob’s arrogance by making their voice so obviously self-important that the reader laughs at them, not with them. The speaker’s condescension (“I do not send postcards of sunsets to those back home”) reveals more about their own insecurity than about the places they visit. The rhyming couplets and controlled stanza structure give the poem a polished, postcard-like surface that reinforces the idea of performance — the speaker is constructing an image of themselves as a superior traveller.

Key Fact

Hannah uses a persona to create dramatic irony: the travel snob thinks they are demonstrating cultural sophistication, but the reader sees through them. The poem is ultimately about how people use place to construct identity — the snob’s destination choices are about ego, not genuine engagement with the world.

Tone: Dickinson’s poem is unsettling and ambiguous; Hannah’s is comic and satirical. Both poets use place to explore something beyond the literal location — Dickinson uses the sea to examine power and vulnerability; Hannah uses travel destinations to examine snobbery and identity performance.

Voice: Dickinson speaks as herself (or a version of herself), making the encounter personal and intimate. Hannah adopts a persona, creating distance between the poet and the speaker. This distance is essential for the satire to work — the reader must recognise that Hannah is mocking, not endorsing, the speaker.

Form: Dickinson’s hymn metre creates a deceptive simplicity that contrasts with the disturbing content. Hannah’s rhyming couplets create a slick, postcard-like surface that mirrors the speaker’s performance of sophistication. Both poets use form ironically — the form says one thing, the content says another.

Connecting to the Wider Anthology

Dickinson pairs well with Davidson (“In Romney Marsh”) — both present nature as an overwhelming force, but Davidson’s speaker is awed while Dickinson’s is threatened. Dickinson also connects to Nichols (“Hurricane Hits England”), where a natural event triggers a deep personal response. Hannah pairs with Afrika (“Nothing’s Changed”) — both poems are about what places reveal about human attitudes, though one is comic and the other is angry.

Displacement & Identity

Some of the most powerful poems in the Time and Place collection come from poets who feel caught between two places, two cultures or two versions of themselves. In this lesson we study three poems about displacement: Alvi’s “Presents from my Aunts in Pakistan,” Nichols’s “Hurricane Hits England” and Adcock’s “Stewart Island.” Each poet uses a specific moment — receiving gifts, surviving a storm, visiting a remote island — to explore larger questions about belonging and identity.

Presents from my Aunts in Pakistan — Moniza Alvi

Alvi was born in Lahore, Pakistan and moved to England as a baby. In this poem, the speaker receives clothes and jewellery from her aunts in Pakistan: a “salwar kameez / peacock-blue,” “gold and black / sari,” bangles and slippers. But the speaker feels conflicted — she “longed / for denim and corduroy” and feels the Pakistani clothes are beautiful but don’t suit her English life. She describes herself as sitting “in the schoolfriend’s house, / of no fixed nationality, / staring through the fretwork.”

The poem is written in free verse with no stanza breaks, mirroring the speaker’s unresolved, flowing thoughts. Alvi uses vivid colour imagery (“peacock-blue,” “apple-green,” “flame-Loss”) for the Pakistani presents, while English items (“denim,” “corduroy,” “cardigans”) are described in plain, colourless terms. This contrast suggests Pakistan is exotic and alluring but also alien, while England is familiar but dull.

Key Fact

Alvi describes herself as “of no fixed nationality” — a phrase that captures the experience of cultural hybridity. She belongs fully to neither Pakistan nor England. The presents from her aunts become symbols of this divided identity: beautiful but uncomfortable, connecting her to a homeland she barely remembers.

Hurricane Hits England — Grace Nichols

Nichols was born in Guyana in the Caribbean and moved to England in 1977. When the Great Storm of October 1987 hit southern England, she experienced an unexpected sense of connection. The hurricane, familiar from her Caribbean childhood, had followed her to England. The poem begins in third person (“It took a hurricane, to bring her closer / To the landscape”) before shifting to first person (“Tell me why you visit / An English coast?”), marking the speaker’s emotional awakening.

Nichols addresses Caribbean storm gods by name — “Huracan,” “Oya,” “Shango” — invoking her cultural heritage and spiritual traditions. The hurricane becomes a bridge between two places: “the earth is the earth is the earth.” This epizeuxis (triple repetition) insists that place is ultimately universal — the same natural forces operate everywhere. By the end, the speaker has resolved her displacement: she belongs in England because the earth itself is connected.

The poem opens with “It took a hurricane, to bring her closer” — “her” distances the speaker from her own experience, as though she is watching herself from outside. When the storm arrives and she addresses the gods directly (“Tell me why you visit”), the pronoun shifts to “me” and “I.” This structural shift mirrors the speaker’s emotional journey: from alienation to ownership of her experience. By the end, speaking in first person, she claims England as her place too.

Stewart Island — Fleur Adcock

Adcock was born in New Zealand but spent most of her adult life in England. “Stewart Island” describes a visit to a remote island off the south coast of New Zealand. The speaker finds a place so untouched and wild that it feels prehistoric: “But for the birds I might have been / the only living creature on the island.” The landscape is beautiful but alienating — the speaker is a visitor, not a native.

The poem uses precise, observational language: “a raft of resting shags,” “silver tree trunks.” Adcock does not romanticise the island; she presents it as real, detailed and slightly uncomfortable. The free verse reflects casual, exploratory thought. Unlike Nichols, who resolves her displacement, Adcock seems to remain an outsider — she appreciates the island’s beauty but does not claim it as home. This reflects her broader position as someone who left New Zealand and never quite returned.

Key Fact

Adcock and Nichols both write as displaced women visiting landscapes connected to their origins, but their conclusions differ. Nichols resolves her displacement through the hurricane (“the earth is the earth is the earth”); Adcock remains an observer, never fully reconnecting with the New Zealand landscape. This makes “Stewart Island” a poem about the impossibility of return.

Identity triggers: Alvi’s displacement is triggered by objects (clothes, jewellery), Nichols’s by a natural event (the hurricane), and Adcock’s by a physical return to a homeland. Each trigger reveals something different about how place shapes identity.

Resolution: Nichols reaches a resolution (“the earth is the earth”); Alvi and Adcock do not. Alvi remains “of no fixed nationality”; Adcock remains a visitor. This makes Nichols’s poem the most optimistic of the three.

Form: All three use free verse, but for different reasons. Alvi’s unbroken flow mirrors unresolved thought; Nichols’s shifting pronouns and invocations create energy and spiritual connection; Adcock’s calm, precise observations keep the reader at a distance, just as the speaker keeps the island at a distance.

86689ccf-2ffb-4d6a-9dc7-c1579371e050.content_html:
“Winter Swans” — Owen Sheers (2005)

Sheers presents a couple whose relationship has been strained. They walk in silence after two days of rain — the pathetic fallacy of the storm mirrors their emotional distance. But when they see swans on a lake, something shifts. The swans “porcelain” their necks towards each other, and the couple begins to reconnect.

The poem’s turning point is nature: the swans model devotion (“they mate for life”), and the couple unconsciously mirror them. The final image — “our hands, like swans, / settled after flight” — is a simile that connects the human and natural. Their hands “settling” suggests the turbulence is over. The form supports this: the poem is written in tercets (three-line stanzas) throughout — an imbalanced number suggesting discord — except the final stanza, which is a couplet (two lines), mirroring the couple coming back together.

Key Fact

Sheers uses form to mirror content: tercets (three-line stanzas = imbalance/discord) shift to a final couplet (two lines = the couple reunited). The swans model natural devotion, and nature heals the relationship. Pathetic fallacy shifts from storm (distance) to calm (reconciliation).

“Climbing My Grandfather” — Andrew Waterhouse (2000)

Waterhouse uses the extended metaphor of mountaineering to explore getting to know his grandfather. The speaker “climbs” the grandfather’s body as if scaling a mountain: “I decide to do it free, without a rope or net” — he approaches the relationship without safety barriers, making himself vulnerable.

Physical details map onto the climbing metaphor: the grandfather’s “earth-stained hand” becomes a handhold, his “still-beating heart” is discovered at the summit: “I place my ear to his chest and I can hear / the distant, accurate, rocking of his heart.” The adjective “accurate” is unusual for a heartbeat — it suggests reliability, precision, and trustworthiness. The journey from base to summit represents deepening emotional knowledge: getting to know someone takes effort, courage, and patience.

Causley’s “Eden Rock” fits the memory and time theme through its gentle re-creation of a childhood scene. The title alludes to the Garden of Eden — a paradise before the Fall, suggesting innocence and perfection. The mundane domestic details (“H.P. Sauce bottle,” “Survey tweed”) anchor the vision in specific, personal memory, making death feel like a return to something known and safe rather than a step into the unknown.

The poem’s pace is slow and deliberate, matching the dreamy quality of the scene. The final line — “I had not thought that it would be like this” — is both a revelation and a comfort. Time dissolves: past, present, and future merge as the speaker approaches the stream (death) with surprising calm.

Key Fact

Waterhouse’s mountaineering metaphor represents the effort of truly knowing someone. The “summit” (the grandfather’s heart) is the emotional core — reaching it requires vulnerability, patience, and physical closeness. The “accurate” heartbeat suggests reliability and trust.

Memory, Time & Connection

These three poems share a focus on how time affects relationships. Sheers shows a relationship healing in the present moment. Waterhouse explores discovery of a person across a lifetime. Causley dissolves time altogether, merging past and present at the threshold of death. All three suggest that love operates across time — it is not confined to a single moment but evolves, deepens, or transcends.

Sheers vs Waterhouse: Both use physical experience to explore emotional connection. Sheers’ couple reconnect through a shared walk (horizontal movement); Waterhouse’s speaker “climbs” to know his grandfather (vertical movement). Both end with discovery: Sheers finds reconciliation, Waterhouse finds the heartbeat.

Waterhouse vs Causley: Both explore grandparental love through physical detail. Waterhouse’s grandfather is alive (the heart still beats); Causley’s parents are dead (but the scene feels alive). Both use mundane detail to make love tangible and real.

Preparing for the Poetry Anthology Exam

This lesson consolidates your revision with key quotations from every poem, a revision strategy, and advice on timing and technique. Use it as a final checkpoint before the exam.

Key Quotations: Love & Relationships

Sonnet 43: “How do I love thee? Let me count the ways” — anaphora builds cumulative intensity. “I love thee to the depth and breadth and height / My soul can reach” — spatial imagery makes love three-dimensional.

She Walks in Beauty: “She walks in beauty, like the night / Of cloudless climes and starry skies” — beauty compared to darkness, not light. “All that’s best of dark and bright / Meet in her aspect” — antithesis creates balance.

Valentine: “Not a red rose or a satin heart” — rejection of cliché. “Its scent will cling to your fingers, / cling to your knife” — love becomes possessive and threatening.

Cozy Apologia: “I could pick anything and think of you” — love permeates ordinary life. “I’m still / as a cicada shell” — outgrown her former self for something real.

The Manhunt: “the damaged, porcelain collar-bone” — fragility beneath toughness. “only then did I come close” — physical and emotional proximity fused.

Key Fact

You need at minimum two quotations per poem for the exam — one for language analysis and one for form/structure. Short quotations (3–7 words) are more effective than long ones because they allow you to analyse individual word choices in detail.

Key Quotations: War & Conflict

Dulce et Decorum Est: “Bent double, like old beggars” — destroys heroic image. “GAS! Gas! Quick, boys!” — sudden panic. “The old Lie: Dulce et decorum est / Pro patria mori” — direct attack on propaganda.

The Soldier: “If I should die, think only this of me” — calm acceptance. “A dust whom England bore, shaped, made aware” — England as nurturing mother.

Mametz Wood: “A mosaic of bone” — fragments are beautiful and terrible. “linked arm in arm” — comradeship persists in death.

A Wife in London: “Flashes of survey” — military language dehumanises loss. “new love” (in the letter) — now impossibly painful because the husband is dead.

Key Quotations: Nature, Power & Time

To Autumn: “Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness” — soft alliteration creates warmth. “sitting careless on a granary floor” — personification of drowsy abundance.

Death of a Naturalist: “Festered in the heart of the townland” — decay as positive (stanza 1). “Gross-bellied frogs were cocked on sods” — military, aggressive, threatening (stanza 2).

The Prelude: “a huge peak, black and huge” — repetition shows overwhelmed state. “Huge and mighty forms… moved slowly through the mind” — nature haunts the boy after the event.

Living Space: “There are just not enough / straight lines” — enjambment mirrors instability. “daring the air to be kind” — fragile hope personified.

Ozymandias: “sneer of cold command” — harsh alliteration reflects cruelty. “Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!” — devastating irony.

London: “mind-forg’d manacles” — mental chains of oppression. “every charter’d street” — ownership and control.

Hawk Roosting: “I kill where I please because it is all mine” — simple, chilling certainty. “No arguments assert my right” — power needs no justification.

Afternoons: “Something is pushing them / To the side of their own lives” — vague agent, passive displacement. “Their beauty has thickened” — time’s subtle physical effect.

As Imperceptibly as Grief: “As imperceptibly as Grief / The Summer lapsed away” — central metaphor. “Into the Beautiful” — loss becomes transcendence.

Step 1: Choose 2–3 quotations per poem (36–54 total). Prioritise quotations you can analyse for multiple effects (language + form + context).

Step 2: For each quotation, write a one-sentence analysis. This becomes your revision flashcard: quotation on one side, analysis on the other.

Step 3: Group quotations by theme (love, power, nature, conflict, time). This mirrors how the exam question will be themed, so you can quickly identify relevant material.

Step 4: Practise writing comparison paragraphs using pairs of quotations. Time yourself: one comparison paragraph should take 5–7 minutes.

Timing and Planning

Key Fact

5 minutes planning: Read the printed poem, identify its key themes and techniques. Choose your comparison poem. Note 3–4 comparison points. 35–40 minutes writing: Introduction (1 paragraph establishing both poems and your argument). 3–4 body paragraphs (alternating structure, both poems in each). Brief conclusion if time allows. Equal coverage: Do not spend significantly more time on one poem than the other.

1. Feature-spotting without analysis: “Owen uses alliteration” earns nothing. Always explain the effect.

2. Retelling the poem: The examiner knows what happens. Focus on how and why the poet presents ideas the way they do.

3. Context as a separate paragraph: Weave context into analysis. “Owen, writing from the trenches, uses graphic imagery to expose the reality that propaganda conceals” is better than a paragraph about World War I with no link to the poem.

4. Only discussing one poem: Both poems must receive substantial treatment. Set a mental alarm: by halfway through your time, you must have discussed both.

5. Long quotations: Quote 3–7 words, then analyse individual words within that quotation. Long quotations waste time and prevent detailed analysis.

Building a Strong Response

The best responses share these qualities: a clear comparative argument stated from the start; quotations embedded smoothly within sentences (not standing alone); analysis at word level (why this word?); awareness of how form and structure contribute to meaning; context woven in to support points rather than bolted on; and a consistent focus on the question’s theme throughout.

When Love Fails

Romantic love does not always last. Three poems in the Relationships collection examine what happens when love fades, fails or becomes something unrecognisable: Wordsworth’s “A Complaint,” Hardy’s “Neutral Tones” and Jennings’s “One Flesh.” Each poet presents disillusionment differently — through loss of emotional connection, through bitter memory, and through the quiet erosion of a marriage — but all three convey the pain of love that no longer sustains.

A Complaint — William Wordsworth (1807)

Wordsworth (1770–1850) is one of the founders of English Romanticism. “A Complaint” is believed to address his friend Samuel Taylor Coleridge, whose emotional withdrawal and opium addiction had strained their friendship. The poem mourns the loss of a deep emotional bond — not a romantic relationship, but a platonic love that was once sustaining and is now reduced to almost nothing.

Key Fact

Wordsworth uses an extended metaphor of a fountain to describe the relationship. It was once “a fountain at my fond heart’s door” that “never ceased to flow” — constant, generous, life-giving. Now it has been replaced by “A well of love — it may be deep — / I trust it is, — and never dry” — a well that may still exist but is hidden, inaccessible and uncertain. The shift from fountain (visible, overflowing) to well (underground, stagnant) captures the devastating change.

Key language: The dashes in “it may be deep — / I trust it is, — and never dry” create hesitation and doubt. The speaker is trying to convince himself that the love still exists, but the broken syntax reveals his uncertainty. The word “trust” is loaded — trust is precisely what has been damaged.

Key structure: The poem has three stanzas: past (the fountain), present (the well), and reflection. This chronological movement from abundance to scarcity mirrors the deterioration of the relationship. The regular metre and rhyme scheme create a controlled, measured tone that contrasts with the emotional pain beneath — Wordsworth keeps his composure even as he mourns.

Neutral Tones — Thomas Hardy (1867)

Hardy (1840–1928) wrote this poem at 27, drawing on a painful romantic experience. It describes a moment when two lovers stand by a pond, recognising that their love is dead. The poem is a memory, recalled years later, and the bitter, stripped-back imagery reflects the speaker’s enduring pain.

Key language: “We stood by a pond that winter day, / And the sun was white, as though chidden of God” — the pathetic fallacy is immediately established. The sun is not warm or golden but “white” and punished (“chidden”), drained of all vitality. The pond, the leaves, the sky — everything in the landscape is bleached and lifeless, reflecting the death of feeling between the lovers.

The simile comparing the lover’s gaze to someone looking at “tedious riddles” is devastating. The word “tedious” suggests boredom and irritation — the speaker has become a puzzle the lover no longer cares to solve. “Rove” implies the eyes wander without focus, suggesting the lover is mentally absent. The speaker is right there, but emotionally the lover has already left.

Key structure: Like Keats’s “La Belle Dame Sans Merci,” Hardy uses a cyclical structure. The poem begins and ends at the pond, with the final stanza: “And a pond edged with greyish leaves.” This return traps the speaker in the memory — he cannot escape the moment when he realised love had died. The four regular quatrains with an ABAB rhyme scheme create a deceptively orderly surface that barely contains the bitterness beneath.

Key Fact

The title “Neutral Tones” is deeply ironic. There is nothing neutral about the poem — it is suffused with bitterness and pain. The “neutral” refers to the drained, colourless landscape and the empty feelings between the lovers, but the speaker’s enduring memory of this moment, decades later, proves that the emotions were anything but neutral.

One Flesh — Elizabeth Jennings (1966)

Jennings (1926–2001) was the only female member of “The Movement,” a group of 1950s English poets who rejected Romantic excess in favour of clarity, restraint and understatement. “One Flesh” describes her elderly parents lying apart in bed, their marriage intact in name but emotionally distant. The title alludes to the Christian marriage vow: “and the two shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24).

Key language: “Lying apart now, each in a separate bed, / He with a survey, she with a book” — the opening is deliberately mundane. The couple is separated physically (different beds) and mentally (different activities). Yet the word “now” implies this was not always the case — the distance has grown over time. “Tossed up like flotsam from a former passion” is a powerful simile: flotsam is wreckage left after a storm, suggesting their current state is the remnant of a love that once had the force of a tempest.

This paradox captures the central mystery of long marriages. The couple are physically and emotionally distant (“apart”), yet bound by decades of shared history (“close together”). The repetition of “strangely” suggests that even the speaker — their own child — cannot fully understand the nature of this bond. It is neither love nor not-love, neither together nor separate. Jennings presents long-term relationships as irreducibly complex.

Key structure: Three regular six-line stanzas with a quiet, understated tone. The regularity of the form mirrors the routine of the couple’s life — predictable, orderly, but lacking passion. The final stanza shifts from observation to reflection: “Whose fire from which I came, has now grown cold?” This question acknowledges that the speaker’s own existence was the product of passion that no longer exists — a deeply unsettling realisation.

Comparing the Three Poems

Different stages of love’s decline: Wordsworth mourns a love that has recently withdrawn (the fountain has just become a well). Hardy bitterly remembers the exact moment love died (by the pond). Jennings observes the long aftermath of love’s slow erosion (her parents in old age). Together, they trace a full arc: loss, death, and the long, quiet aftermath.

Tone contrast: Wordsworth is measured and controlled; Hardy is bitter and ironic; Jennings is contemplative and sad. These tonal differences reflect different relationships with disappointment — Wordsworth still hopes, Hardy has given up, Jennings simply observes with quiet puzzlement.
